title: Directive Principles & Fundamental Duties
summary: What the State should aim for (Part IV), how it clashes with rights, and the citizen's duties.

subcards.title: Directive Principles: meaning, features and classification
subcards.summary: What Part IV tells the State to aim for, and how it is grouped.
at_a_glance: Instrument of Instructions, Government of India Act 1935
Non-justiciable (courts cannot enforce them), but fundamental in the governance of the country (Art 37)
Welfare state; social and economic democracy
Socialistic, Gandhian, liberal-intellectual (made by scholars; the Constitution does not group them)
Art 335, Art 350A and Art 351 are directives placed in other Parts

blocks.title: Basic facts
head: Point
Fact
rows: Part IV of the Constitution, Article 36 to Article 51. The actual directives are in Art 38 to Art 51; Art 36 defines "State" and Art 37 explains their nature.
Irish Constitution of 1937. Ireland had itself copied the idea from the Spanish Constitution.

They resemble the "Instrument of Instructions" in the Government of India Act, 1935. Ambedkar: Directive Principles are "merely another name for the instrument of instructions"; the only difference is that they are instructions to the legislature and the executive (the old ones went to the Governor-General and Governors).

Their origin is also traced to the Karachi Resolution of the Indian National Congress (1931) and to the socialist and nationalist ideas common in India from the 1920s. Gandhian ideas also shaped them. (This point is not in Laxmikanth, but it is asked in previous exam questions.)
Ideals that the State must keep in mind while making policies and laws. They are constitutional instructions to the State in legislative, executive and administrative matters.

Same meaning as in Part III (Art 12): Union and state governments and legislatures, all local authorities and all other public authorities. So they guide every level of government, not only the Union.

A "welfare state" (a State that looks after people's well-being), not a "police state" (a State that only keeps law and order and defends borders, as in colonial times). They aim at social and economic democracy.

blocks.title: Key features
items: Non-justiciable (not enforceable in a court): no court can enforce them, so no government (Central, state or local) can be forced by a court to implement them.
Yet Art 37 says they are "fundamental in the governance of the country" and it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.
They are a full economic, social and political programme. They aim at the Preamble's ideals of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.
Economic justice, as an objective, is found in the Preamble and in the Directive Principles.
They help courts: if a law gives effect to a Directive Principle, a court may treat that law as "reasonable" under Art 14 or Art 19 and save it from being struck down (cancelled).
Along with the Fundamental Rights, they contain the philosophy (soul) of the Constitution.
Like the Preamble and the Fundamental Duties, they reflect ideas of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948).

blocks.title: Which Part holds what (often mixed up)
head: Part
Contents
rows: Fundamental Rights, e.g. Art 17 untouchability abolished, Art 18 titles abolished, Art 21 life and personal liberty, Art 24 no child below 14 in factories
Fundamental Duties (added in 1976; not in the 1950 Constitution)
Elections: right to vote on the basis of adult suffrage

blocks.title: Who decided and why
items: Sir B.N. Rau, Constitutional Advisor to the Constituent Assembly, recommended dividing rights into two kinds: justiciable (court-enforceable) and non-justiciable. The Drafting Committee accepted this. Justiciable rights went into Part III; non-justiciable principles went into Part IV.
Reason 1: India did not have enough money to carry them out.
Reason 2: India's vast diversity and backwardness would stand in the way.
Reason 3: the newly independent State had many burdens, so it needed freedom to decide the order, time, place and way of fulfilling them (flexibility).
Making Part IV safe from constitutional amendment was NOT a reason.

blocks.title: What force they have, then
items: Moral and political sanction, not legal sanction. The real force is public opinion.
Ambedkar: a government resting on popular vote cannot ignore them; if it does, it must answer to the electorate at election time.
Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar: no ministry responsible to the people can lightly ignore Part IV.
Positive in nature: they ask the State to DO things (Fundamental Rights are negative: they stop the State from doing things).
They promote the welfare of the whole community, so they are societarian (community-centred) and socialistic. Fundamental Rights promote the welfare of the individual.
They need laws to be implemented; they are not automatically enforced.
They are not limits on the legislature or the executive; they are guides to both.
A law cannot be struck down only because it goes against a Directive Principle. Art 13 makes void (cancels) laws that violate Part III (Fundamental Rights), not laws that go against Part IV.
They cannot be enforced by moving the Supreme Court under Art 32 (that remedy is for Fundamental Rights only).

They do not override Fundamental Rights. But Parliament CAN amend Fundamental Rights in order to implement them, as long as it does not damage the basic structure (the core features) of the Constitution.

To change the text of a Directive Principle, Parliament must pass a constitutional amendment by special majority under Art 368. Ratification (approval) by half of the state legislatures is not needed just because the provision is in Part IV.

blocks.title: What each Article says
head: Article
What it directs
Group
rows: Definition of "State": same as in Part III
Not enforceable by any court, but fundamental in the governance of the country. It is the State's duty to apply them in making laws
Promote people's welfare by securing a social order with justice: social, economic and political

Minimise inequalities in income, and remove inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities, among individuals and also among groups living in different areas or doing different jobs (added by 44th Amendment, 1978)
Adequate means of livelihood for all citizens, men and women equally (not identical income for all)
Ownership and control of the community's material resources distributed to best serve the common good
Economic system must not cause concentration of wealth and means of production to the common harm
Equal pay for equal work for both men and women

The health and strength of workers (men and women) and the tender age of children must not be abused, and citizens must not be forced by economic need to take up work unsuited to their age or strength

Children must get opportunities and facilities to develop in a healthy way, in conditions of freedom and dignity, and childhood and youth must be protected from exploitation and from moral and material abandonment (being left without care or support). Added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976

The legal system must promote justice on the basis of equal opportunity. The State must provide free legal aid so that no citizen is denied justice because of economic or other disabilities. It is not limited to criminal cases (added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976)
Organise village panchayats and give them powers to work as units of self-government

Within the limits of its economic capacity and development, the State shall secure the right to work, the right to education, and public assistance in unemployment, old age, sickness, disablement and other cases of undeserved want (need that is not the person's fault). The 'economic capacity' limit applies to all three (work, education, assistance), not only to assistance
Just and humane conditions of work, and maternity relief
Living wage, a decent standard of life, full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities for all workers
Promote cottage industries in rural areas, on an individual or co-operative basis (no government ownership needed)
Workers' participation in the management of industries (added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976)
Voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies (added by 97th Amendment, 2011)
Uniform civil code for citizens throughout India

Early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years (present form, 86th Amendment, 2002). Original Art 45: free and compulsory education for all children up to 14 years, within 10 years of the Constitution's start
Promote with special care the educational and economic interests of weaker sections, especially SCs and STs, and protect them from social injustice and all exploitation
The State must treat raising the level of nutrition and the standard of living of its people, and improving public health, as among its primary duties
Prohibit intoxicating drinks and drugs harmful to health, except for medicinal purposes (no separate industrial exception)
Organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines
Preserve and improve cattle breeds; prohibit slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle
Protect and improve the environment, and safeguard forests and wildlife (added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976)

Protect every monument, place or object of artistic or historic interest that is declared to be of national importance by or under a law made by Parliament, from spoliation (damage or plunder), disfigurement, destruction, removal, disposal or export. A building is not covered just because it is old
Separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State

(a) promote international peace and security; (b) keep just and honourable relations between nations; (c) foster respect for international law and treaty obligations; (d) encourage settling international disputes by arbitration. It does NOT give treaties automatic legal force
blocks.note: No Article of Part IV has ever been omitted. Art 45 was substituted (rewritten), not removed. A "living wage" is more than a "minimum wage": a minimum wage covers only bare food, shelter and clothing, while a living wage also covers education, health and insurance. A "fair wage" lies between the two. Previous exam questions link Community Development Programmes (launched to raise the standard of living) to Art 47.

blocks.title: Things NOT in Part IV (common wrong options)
items: Abolition of untouchability (Art 17), protection of minorities, and life and personal liberty (Art 21) are Fundamental Rights, not Directive Principles.
Ban on traffic in human beings (buying and selling people) and forced labour (Art 23) is a Fundamental Right.
Protection of personal law and increasing international trade are not Directive Principles at all.
Free and compulsory education for children of 6 to 14 years is now a Fundamental Right (Art 21A), not a Directive Principle.

blocks.text: see Implementation of Directive Principles (laws and schemes for each Article)
The Constitution itself does NOT classify them. This three-way grouping is made by scholars, based on content.

children.label: Socialistic (social and economic justice, welfare state)
Art 46 weaker sections, SCs and STs
Art 48 ban on cow slaughter, better breeds
Art 48 scientific agriculture and animal husbandry

blocks.title: Split Articles (one Article, two groups)
items: Art 43: the living-wage part is Socialistic; the cottage-industries part is Gandhian.
Art 47: the nutrition and public-health part is Socialistic; the prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs is Gandhian.
Art 48: the scientific-agriculture part is Liberal-intellectual; the ban on cow slaughter is Gandhian.

sections.heading: Amendments that added or changed Directive Principles

blocks.title: Changes to Part IV, in order
head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: Added FOUR new directives: Art 39(f) healthy development of children, Art 39A equal justice and free legal aid, Art 43A workers in management, Art 48A environment, forests and wildlife
Added Art 38(2): minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities

Changed Art 45 to early childhood care and education up to age six. The same Amendment made elementary education (6 to 14 years) a Fundamental Right in Art 21A, and added Fundamental Duty Art 51A(k): a parent or guardian must give a child of 6 to 14 years opportunities for education. This parental duty does not remove the State's own duty under Art 21A

Added Art 43B on co-operative societies. The same Amendment made forming co-operative societies a Fundamental Right (Art 19(1)(c)) and added a new Part IX-B "The Co-operative Societies" (Art 243ZH to 243ZT). Note: it is Part IX-B, not Part X-B

blocks.title: Other 42nd Amendment ("Mini-Constitution") facts asked with this
items: Added Part IVA (Fundamental Duties) and Part XIV-A (Tribunals: Art 323A administrative tribunals, Art 323B other tribunals).
Moved education and four other subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List (the list on which both Parliament and state legislatures can make laws).
Replacing "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion" in Art 352 was done by the 44th Amendment (1978), not the 42nd.
Free and compulsory education for 6 to 14 was made a Fundamental Right by the 86th Amendment, not the 76th.

blocks.text: see how the 42nd Amendment widened Art 31C

blocks.title: Directives in other Parts
head: Article
Part
What it says
rows: The claims of Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) to jobs in Union and state services must be taken into account, in a way that keeps administration efficient
Every state and local authority should provide instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children of linguistic minorities
Union's duty to spread and develop Hindi as a medium of expression of India's composite culture
blocks.note: These too are non-justiciable (courts cannot enforce them), but courts give them the same importance as Part IV directives, because all parts of the Constitution are read together.

blocks.title: Who said what
head: Person
Said Directive Principles are…
rows: A "novel feature" of the Constitution; their value is that they set "economic democracy" (as different from political democracy) as the goal
With Fundamental Rights, the "conscience of the Constitution"; "aimed at furthering the goals of the social revolution"
"Moral precepts for the authorities of the State"; they have at least an educative value
"Pious superfluities"; like "a cheque on a bank, payable only when the resources of the bank permit"
No better than New Year's resolutions, broken on the second of January
"Manifesto of aims and aspirations"; they serve as a mere "moral homily" (moral lecture)

"Pious aspirations" (good wishes only). He said they have no consistent philosophy and are conservative, being based on 19th-century English political thinking: "Fabian Socialism without the socialism"
Neither properly classified nor logically arranged
They can cause constitutional conflict: between the Centre and the states, between the President and the Prime Minister, and between the Governor and the Chief Minister
If fully carried out, India would be "a heaven on earth"

blocks.title: Four criticisms (Laxmikanth headings)
items: No legal force
Illogically arranged
Conservative
Constitutional conflict
Note: 'they make Fundamental Rights non-justiciable' is NOT a criticism, because they do no such thing.

blocks.title: Utility
items: M.C. Setalvad said they are like an Instrument of Instructions to all authorities; they are beacon-lights (guiding lights) for courts in judicial review (checking whether laws are valid); they form the background to all State action; and they amplify (explain in detail) the Preamble.
Give stability and continuity to policy even when the ruling party changes.
Supplement Fundamental Rights by providing social and economic rights; their implementation helps people truly enjoy Fundamental Rights.
They let the opposition criticise the government, and let people judge the government's performance against them.
Act as a common political manifesto for any ruling party.
They do NOT empower courts to enforce them.
Part IV is Art 36 to 51 (Part V is 'The Union', a common wrong option). Source: Ireland's Constitution (1937), which itself copied Spain's.
Art 37 says two things together: they are not enforceable by courts, BUT they are fundamental in the governance of the country. Both are true.
Village panchayats = Art 40 (not Art 243, 73 or 74). Uniform civil code = Art 44. Judiciary separate from executive = Art 50. International peace and arbitration = Art 51.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) added FOUR: Art 39(f), 39A, 43A and 48A. Art 38(2) came in 1978 (44th Amendment), the new Art 45 in 2002 (86th Amendment), and Art 43B in 2011 (97th Amendment).
Art 39A is free legal aid; Art 43A is workers' participation in management. Exams swap these two.
Art 46 (SCs, STs, weaker sections) and Art 43B (co-operatives) are Gandhian, not socialistic.
Art 39(b) and Art 39(c) together express distributive justice (fair sharing): resources must serve the common good, and wealth must not be concentrated in a few hands.

Who said what: 'novel feature' was Ambedkar; 'conscience of the Constitution' was Granville Austin; 'moral precepts' was B.N. Rau; 'cheque on a bank' was K.T. Shah; 'dustbin of sentiments' was T.T. Krishnamachari; 'New Year resolutions' was Nasiruddin; 'pious aspirations' was Ivor Jennings.

subcards.title: Implementation of Directive Principles
subcards.summary: Which laws and schemes put each Directive Principle into practice.
at_a_glance: Directive Principles (DPSPs) cannot be enforced in court, so governments carry them out through laws and schemes
Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 (in force 9 November 1995)
73rd Amendment Act 1992 gave panchayats constitutional status
Goa has had one since Portuguese rule; Uttarakhand UCC in force from 27 January 2025
Non-alignment (not joining any power bloc) and Panchsheel (five principles of peaceful coexistence)
Lack of money, poor social and economic conditions, population growth, and strained relations between the Centre and the States

sections.heading: Laws and schemes Article by Article

blocks.text: Since 1950 the Centre and the States have passed many laws and started many programmes to carry out the Directive Principles. Main examples (Laxmikanth):

blocks.title: Each Directive Principle and the law or scheme that implements it
head: Article (what it asks)
Laws, bodies and schemes
rows: Planning Commission (set up 1950) and the Five Year Plans. NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015.

Land reforms in almost all States: abolition of zamindars, jagirdars and inamdars (middlemen); tenancy reforms (security of tenure, fair rent); ceilings on land holdings; giving surplus land to landless labourers; cooperative farming
Nationalisation of life insurance (1956), 14 big commercial banks (1969), general insurance (1971); abolition of Privy Purses (1971) (yearly payments to former rulers of princely States)
Art 39(d) (equal pay for equal work for men and women)
Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986. In 2016 it was renamed the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986. Child labour was banned in 2006.

Minimum Wages Act 1948, Payment of Wages Act 1936, Payment of Bonus Act 1965, Factories Act 1948, Mines Act 1952, Industrial Disputes Act 1947, Trade Unions Act 1926, Workmen's Compensation Act 1923, Contract Labour Act 1970, Bonded Labour System Abolition Act 1976
Khadi and Village Industries Commission, Small-Scale Industries Board, National Small Industries Corporation, Handloom Board, Handicrafts Board, Coir Board, Silk Board

Community Development Programme (1952), Hill Area Development Programme (1960), Drought-Prone Area Programme (1973), Minimum Needs Programme (1974), Integrated Rural Development Programme (1978), Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (1989), Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (1999), Sampoorna Grameena Rozgar Yojana (2001), National Rural Employment Guarantee Programme (2006)
Legal Services Authorities Act 1987; Lok Adalats
Three-tier panchayati raj (village, taluka and district levels); 73rd Amendment Act 1992

Reservations in education, jobs and legislatures; Protection of Civil Rights Act (the Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955, renamed in 1976); SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989; National Commission for SCs and STs (65th Amendment 1990), split into two by 89th Amendment 2003; National Commissions for Women (1992), Backward Classes (1993), Minorities (1993), Child Rights (2007); constitutional status to Backward Classes Commission by 102nd Amendment 2018; 10% EWS (Economically Weaker Sections) reservation 2019 (103rd Amendment)
Primary health centres and hospitals; programmes against malaria, TB, leprosy, AIDS and other diseases
Modern seeds, fertilisers and irrigation; cow, calf and bullock slaughter banned by laws in some States
Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972; Forest (Conservation) Act 1980; Water and Air Acts (set up Central and State Pollution Control Boards); National Forest Policy 1988
Ancient and Historical Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act 1951
Policy of non-alignment (not joining any power bloc) and Panchsheel (five principles of peaceful coexistence)
Old-age pension schemes in some States for people above 65 years

blocks.text: Even so, Directive Principles are not fully carried out. Reasons given by Laxmikanth: not enough money, unfavourable social and economic conditions, population explosion, and strained Centre–State relations.
For what each Article (Art 38–51) says and which Amendment added it, see Directive Principles: meaning, features and classification

blocks.title: Recent laws (as of Nov 2026)
head: Law
Key facts
Directive Principle
rows: Code on Wages 2019; Industrial Relations Code 2020; Code on Social Security 2020; Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020. Together they replace 29 central labour laws. In force from 21 November 2025. (There is no 'Code on Employment Guarantee'.)
Gave the right-to-work directive of Art 41 the form of a law (100 days of wage work for a rural household)
Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act 2025 (short name VB–G RAM G; rozgar = employment, ajeevika = livelihood, gramin = rural)
Replaced MGNREGA from 1 July 2026; guarantees 125 days of wage work in a year to rural households
Gives subsidised food grains; carries out the goal of Art 47 (nutrition and standard of living)
blocks.note: These laws give a legal right to work or food, but the right to work is still NOT a Fundamental Right in Part III.

blocks.title: Key facts
items: Labour subjects (industrial and labour disputes, social security, welfare of labour) are in the Concurrent List (List III of the Seventh Schedule). So both Parliament and State Legislatures can make laws on them — they are NOT in the Union List.

National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (NCRWC, 2002): recommended a new Fundamental Right to rural wage employment for at least 80 days a year. This would bind the State to secure rural wage employment by a suitable law.
Art 39(e): the State must ensure that citizens are not forced by economic need to enter work unsuited to their age or strength — this is the directive that fits children forced into unsuitable work.
The aim behind all these schemes (livelihood, education, health, lower inequality) is a welfare State with social and economic democracy.

blocks.title: Cases
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: A Kerala law giving extra paid national and festival holidays to workers was upheld. The Supreme Court used Art 43 (living wage and decent conditions of work) to decide whether this limit on the employer's freedom of business under Art 19(1)(g) was a reasonable restriction under Art 19(6).
A Directive Principle helps decide 'reasonableness'; it does NOT make a welfare law immune from Fundamental Rights review.
K. Umadevi v. Government of Tamil Nadu (May 2025)

A Tamil Nadu government employee already had two children from her first marriage. She was refused maternity leave for a child from her second marriage, because a State rule allowed it only to women with fewer than two surviving children. The Supreme Court set aside the refusal.
Maternity benefits are part of a woman's reproductive rights under Art 21 (right to life and personal liberty). The Court did not strike down all two-child rules.

blocks.title: Social justice laws that courts uphold
items: Courts uphold social-justice laws that: remove economic inequality; give working people a decent standard of living; protect weaker sections.
Courts do NOT uphold laws that claim to be 'unquestionable' or beyond any judicial review, because judicial review (the courts' power to test laws) is part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

sections.heading: Legal aid (Art 39A) and separation of judiciary (Art 50)

blocks.title: Article 39A
items: Art 39A: the State shall make sure the legal system promotes justice on the basis of equal opportunity, and shall provide free legal aid so that no citizen is denied justice because of economic or other disabilities.
Added by the 42nd Amendment Act 1976. It is a Directive Principle, not a Fundamental Right.
It is NOT limited to criminal cases.
Do not mix up: Art 39A is free legal aid; Art 43A is workers' participation in the management of industries. Both were added by the 42nd Amendment.

items.detail: Early expert report on legal aid to the poor

items.what: First Lok Adalat camp after Independence, in Gujarat
Legal Services Authorities Act passed by Parliament
The Act comes into force; NALSA (National Legal Services Authority) set up under it

blocks.title: Legal Services Authorities Act and Lok Adalat
items: Builds a nation-wide network: NALSA at the top; State Legal Services Authority in each State; High Court Legal Services Committee; District Legal Services Authorities; Taluk Legal Services Committees.
Lok Adalat ('people's court') is a forum set up by law (a statutory forum) where disputes are settled by compromise between the parties. It has the status of a civil court.
A Lok Adalat award is binding on the parties and final — no appeal lies to any court against it.
Justice P.N. Bhagwati popularised the Lok Adalat and legal aid movement.
Law Commission's 114th Report recommended Gram Nyayalayas (village courts) — basis of the Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008.
Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended administrative tribunals — they came in as Part XIV-A (Art 323A, 323B) through the 42nd Amendment.

blocks.title: Case
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Suk Das v. Union Territory of Arunachal Pradesh (1986)
A poor accused was convicted without a lawyer; the court had not told him he could get free legal aid. Conviction set aside.
Not applying for legal aid does not excuse the court's failure to inform him. Free legal aid is part of a fair trial under Art 21.

blocks.title: Article 50 — separation of judiciary from executive
items: Art 50 (a Directive Principle, Part IV): the State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
It separates the judiciary from the executive. It is NOT about separating the legislature from the executive, and NOT about Union and State judicial services.

Implemented by the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) 1973. Before this Code, executive officers such as the collector, sub-divisional officer and tehsildar also held judicial powers. After it, these judicial powers went to judicial magistrates, who work under the control of the State High Court.
Separation of judiciary from executive is required by the Directive Principles — not by the Preamble, the Seventh Schedule or mere convention.

blocks.title: Articles often matched with Art 50
head: Article
What it deals with
rows: Directive Principle: separate judiciary from executive
Executive power of the Union vested in the President
High Court's superintendence (supervision) over all courts in its territory
Allows creation of All India Services, including an All India Judicial Service

blocks.title: Education
items: 86th Amendment Act 2002 (not the 76th) made elementary education for children aged 6 to 14 a Fundamental Right under Art 21A. It also changed Art 45 so that it now asks for early childhood care and education up to age 6.
42nd Amendment 1976 moved education from the State List to the Concurrent List.
Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan also aims at computer education, even in rural areas.
Provisions bearing on education are spread across the Constitution: Directive Principles, rural and urban local bodies, Fifth Schedule, Sixth Schedule and Seventh Schedule.
Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act 2009 — in force from 1 April 2010 (with the 86th Amendment).

RTE Act: at least three-fourths of the members of a School Management Committee must be parents or guardians of the children. The Act bans capitation fees (extra donation money taken for admission) and screening (tests or interviews of the child or parents) for admission.
2019 amendment to RTE Act: States may now hold back (detain) children in Classes 5 and 8 if they fail a re-exam — so the 'no detention' rule is no longer absolute.

blocks.title: RTE Act cases
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012)
Upheld the RTE Act, including the duty of private unaided schools (not run by minorities) to admit children from weaker sections (25% quota)
Private schools also share the duty to educate
Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014)
A Constitution Bench (five or more judges) held that the RTE Act cannot apply to minority schools protected by Art 30(1), whether aided or unaided
Minority schools are outside the RTE Act

blocks.title: Environment (Art 48A) — cases and principles
head: Case or principle (year)
Held or means
Why it matters
rows: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996)
Precautionary principle and polluter-pays principle are essential parts of sustainable development and part of Indian law
Under the precautionary principle, the burden of proof is on the developer: he must show the activity is safe for the environment
Public trust doctrine is part of the law of the land; a motel lease on ecologically fragile land by the Beas river was set aside
The State holds natural resources (rivers, forests) as a trustee for the public and must justify giving them to private use
Lack of full scientific certainty is NOT a reason to postpone steps against serious, irreversible harm
Prevent harm first; do not wait for full scientific proof
The polluter must pay compensation and also the cost of restoring the environment
Protect the interests of future generations

blocks.title: Environment laws and Articles
items: Art 48A was NOT in the original Constitution; the 42nd Amendment (1976) added it. It asks the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife.
Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 was renamed in 2023 as the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980. It also supports the Fundamental Duty in Art 51A(g).

blocks.title: Cattle (Art 48)
items: Art 48: organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern, scientific lines; preserve and improve breeds; prohibit slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle.
So protection is NOT limited to cows and calves — it covers other milch (milk-giving) and draught (load-pulling) cattle too.
Art 48 is about cattle and agriculture; Art 48A is about environment, forests and wildlife.

The Centre's power to make laws on cattle protection comes from Entry 17 of the Concurrent List (List III): 'Prevention of cruelty to animals'. Art 48 itself gives no law-making power, because Directive Principles only guide the State.

blocks.title: Village panchayats (Art 40)
items: Art 40: the State shall organise village panchayats and give them powers needed to work as units of self-government.
It is a Gandhian principle. It was implemented through three-tier panchayati raj and the 73rd Amendment Act 1992, which added Part IX (Art 243 onwards).
In exam answer keys, the Community Development Programme (1952) is linked to Art 47 (raising the standard of living).

blocks.text: For Champakam Dorairajan, Golaknath, Kesavananda and Unni Krishnan on Fundamental Rights vs Directive Principles, see Fundamental Rights vs Directive Principles

blocks.title: What it is
items: Art 44: 'The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.' It is a Directive Principle (in the liberal-intellectual group), not a Fundamental Right.
A Uniform Civil Code (UCC) means one common set of personal laws for all citizens, whatever their religion — on marriage, divorce, inheritance, adoption and maintenance.
It would replace religion-based personal laws (for example the Hindu Marriage Act and Muslim Personal Law). It has nothing to do with criminal law, tax or trade.
'Protection of personal law' is NOT a Directive Principle.

blocks.title: States with a UCC (as of Nov 2026)
head: State
Status
rows: Has had a common civil code since Portuguese rule (Portuguese Civil Code of 1867), kept after Goa joined India in 1961. It applies to all communities, whatever their religion.

Uniform Civil Code, Uttarakhand, 2024: passed by the Assembly February 2024; President's assent March 2024; in force from 27 January 2025. First State after Independence to enact and enforce a UCC. Scheduled Tribes are kept out.

UCC Bill passed by the Assembly in March 2026; President's assent 17 September 2026. Second State after Uttarakhand to get a UCC law. It comes into force only from a date the State Government notifies. Scheduled Tribes are kept out.

UCC Bill passed by the Assembly on 27 May 2026; President's assent 29 September 2026. A panel is drafting the rules, and the law comes into force only from a date the State Government notifies. Scheduled Tribes are kept out.
blocks.note: Madhya Pradesh: the Assembly passed its UCC Bill on 21 July 2026 (Scheduled Tribes kept out). It is not counted in this table because its assent and start date were not confirmed as of Nov 2026.

blocks.title: Law Commission
items: October 2016: the Law Commission of India (21st Law Commission) issued a public questionnaire on the UCC.
2018: its consultation paper said a UCC was 'neither necessary nor desirable' at that stage and suggested reforming family laws instead.
June 2023: the 22nd Law Commission again invited public views on a UCC.

blocks.title: Cases on Art 44 and personal law
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Shah Bano case (1985) (Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum)

Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 (maintenance for wives, children and parents) is secular and applies to people of all religions. A Muslim husband must pay maintenance to his divorced wife beyond the iddat period (about three months after divorce) if she cannot maintain herself. Mahr (dower) does not free him from this.
Her religion alone did not shut her out of Section 125. Court said a UCC would help national integration. Led to the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986.
Upheld the 1986 Act, but read it to mean the husband must make fair provision for her even beyond iddat
So the relief given in Shah Bano continued
A Hindu husband who converts to Islam and marries again without dissolving his first marriage: the second marriage is invalid
Conversion cannot be used to escape the law of the first marriage. Court urged the government to frame a UCC.
Pannalal Bansilal Pitti v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1996)
A law reforming one community's religious endowments is valid even if other communities' laws are not reformed at the same time
Reform can come step by step; a UCC need not come all at once
John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003)
Struck down Section 118 of the Indian Succession Act (which limited Christians' gifts to charity in a will)
Court again regretted that Art 44 had not been implemented

Talaq-e-biddat (instant triple talaq) was set aside by a 3:2 majority. The judges gave different reasons; Laxmikanth records it as violating Art 14 because it is manifestly arbitrary (clearly unreasonable).
Led to the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act 2019 (Triple Talaq Act)
blocks.note: Landmark UCC judgments to remember: Shah Bano and Sarla Mudgal. Kesavananda Bharati is about basic structure, not UCC.

blocks.title: Article 51 — the State shall endeavour to:
items: (a) promote international peace and security;
(b) maintain just and honourable relations between nations;
(c) foster respect for international law and treaty obligations;
(d) encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration — this is Art 51(d).
Art 51 does NOT make treaties automatically part of Indian law; Parliament must still make a law to implement a treaty (Art 253).
Promotion of international peace is in the Directive Principles — not in the Preamble, Fundamental Duties or Ninth Schedule.
Implemented by India's policy of non-alignment and Panchsheel.
Art 39A (free legal aid) and Art 48A (environment) were added by the 42nd Amendment 1976 — not in the original Constitution.
Legal Services Authorities Act: passed 1987, in force 9 November 1995.
Art 50 (separate the judiciary from the executive) was implemented by the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973. Art 40 (village panchayats) was implemented by the 73rd Amendment 1992.
Art 44 is about the Uniform Civil Code (UCC). Goa has a common civil code from Portuguese times; Uttarakhand is the first State to enact one after Independence (in force 27 January 2025).
The UCC questionnaire of October 2016 was issued by the Law Commission of India.
Art 51(d) is about settling international disputes by arbitration. Art 51 does not make treaties automatically part of Indian law.
Art 39(d) gives equal pay for equal work; the Constitution does not define 'backward classes'.
VB–G RAM G Act 2025 replaced MGNREGA from 1 July 2026 (125 days), but the right to work is still not a Fundamental Right.

subcards.title: Fundamental Rights vs Directive Principles
subcards.summary: How Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles differ, clashed, and are balanced today.
at_a_glance: Part III (Fundamental Rights) and Part IV (Directive Principles)
Art 37: Directive Principles cannot be enforced by any court, but they are fundamental in the governance of the country
Art 31C: protects some laws that implement Directive Principles from challenge under Art 14 and Art 19
Champakam Dorairajan case (1951): Fundamental Rights prevail
Golaknath case (1967): Parliament cannot take away or reduce Fundamental Rights by amendment
Minerva Mills case (1980): the balance between the two is part of the basic structure
Fundamental Rights are supreme. But Parliament can amend them to implement Directive Principles, as long as the basic structure is not harmed

sections.heading: Fundamental Rights vs Directive Principles: the differences

blocks.title: Laxmikanth Table 9.1
head: Aspect
Fundamental Rights (Part III)
Directive Principles (Part IV)
rows: Negative: they stop the State from doing certain things
Positive: they ask the State to do certain things
Justiciable: courts can enforce them if they are violated
Moral and political sanction (no legal sanction)
The individual, so they are personal and individualistic
The community, so they are societarian (society-centred) and socialistic
Yes. They need legislation (a law) to be implemented
Courts must strike down a law that violates a Fundamental Right
Courts cannot strike down a law only because it violates a Directive Principle. But courts can uphold (save) a law because it was made to give effect to a Directive Principle

blocks.title: Small but tested points
items: Some Fundamental Rights work against private persons also, not only against the State. Examples: Art 15(2) (no one may be denied access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, wells and similar places), Art 17 (abolition of untouchability), Art 23 (ban on forced labour) and Art 24 (ban on child labour in factories).
Art 37 itself says two things: Directive Principles cannot be enforced by any court, AND it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.

Directive Principles supplement Fundamental Rights: they add social and economic rights, so that people can really enjoy their freedoms (for example, nutrition, education and livelihood help the poor use their rights).
Directive Principles do not give any enforceable right. A breach of a Directive Principle does not make a law invalid.

Directive Principles do not restrict (limit) the law-making (legislative) or executive power of the State; they are only guidelines for both. In UPSC 2017, the correct answer to 'Do they limit legislative and executive functions?' was 'Neither'.

Amending a Directive Principle needs the Article 368 special majority in each House of Parliament (a majority of the total membership of the House, and two-thirds of the members present and voting). Approval (ratification) by the States is not needed just because the provision is in Part IV.
Fundamental Duties were not put in Part III because Part III is justiciable (enforceable in court), while duties are not.

blocks.text: see Directive Principles: meaning, features and classification (Art 37 in detail)

items.detail: If Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles conflict, Fundamental Rights prevail. Directive Principles must 'conform to and run as subsidiary to' (follow and stay below) Fundamental Rights. But the Court said Parliament can change Fundamental Rights by a constitutional amendment.
Added Art 15(4), Art 31A, Art 31B and the Ninth Schedule.
Parliament's amending power under Art 368 includes the power to amend Fundamental Rights.

More amendments to implement Directive Principles. The 17th Amendment added a safeguard to Art 31A: if the State takes land that a person cultivates himself and that is within the ceiling limit (maximum land allowed), it must pay compensation at market value.
Upheld the 17th Amendment and repeated Shankari Prasad: Parliament can amend Part III.
Fundamental Rights are 'sacrosanct' (sacred). Parliament cannot take away or abridge them, even to implement Directive Principles.
Parliament can abridge or take away any Fundamental Right by a constitutional amendment.
Inserted Article 31C (see next section).
Struck down the second part of Art 31C (which stopped courts from checking whether the law really served the policy). Upheld the first part.
Extended Art 31C protection to laws implementing ANY Directive Principle, not just Art 39(b) and (c).
Removed the right to property (Art 31 and Art 19(1)(f)) from Part III. Because Art 31 was deleted, the mention of Art 31 inside Art 31C also went.
Struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Art 31C. Held that the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is part of the basic structure.

items.what: Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra
items.detail: Nine-judge bench. All nine judges held that Art 31C, in the form upheld in Kesavananda, still operates. By 8 to 1, it held that not every privately owned resource is a 'material resource of the community' under Art 39(b).

blocks.title: Cases
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: The Madras 'Communal G.O.' (Government Order giving caste-based seats in medical and engineering colleges) violated Art 15(1) and Art 29(2). Art 46 (a Directive Principle) could not override these rights.
First case on the conflict: Fundamental Rights prevail. To answer it, the 1st Amendment added Art 15(4).
Parliament's power under Art 368 includes amending Fundamental Rights. The word 'law' in Art 13 means only ordinary law, not a constitutional amendment.
Parliament could amend Part III (Fundamental Rights).
Courts should apply harmonious construction: give effect to both Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles as far as possible.
Sajjan Singh case (1964; some books write 1965, the year it was reported)
Upheld the 17th Amendment and said Parliament can amend Part III.
Parliament cannot take away or abridge (reduce) Fundamental Rights, even to implement Directive Principles. Used prospective overruling (new rule applies only to the future).
Did NOT say Directive Principles are enforceable. Parliament replied with the 24th and 25th Amendments.
Second part of Art 31C is invalid, because judicial review (courts checking laws) is a basic feature. First part is valid. Parliament's amending power cannot alter the basic structure.
Art 31C survives, but only its first part.
The 42nd Amendment's extension of Art 31C is invalid. Also struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Art 368, which the 42nd Amendment had added.
The balance between Part III and Part IV is part of the basic structure.
Laws put in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda judgment) are valid only if they do not damage the basic structure.
Ninth Schedule laws do not get blanket (total) immunity. Laws added after 24 April 1973 can be tested against Art 14, Art 15, Art 19, Art 21 and the basic structure.
Judicial review is a basic feature.

blocks.title: Prospective overruling (used in Golaknath case)
items: Meaning: the court gives a new rule that applies only to the future, so past actions stay valid.
It comes from American law. The Golaknath case (1967) first used it in India.
Because of this, the 1st (1951), 4th (1955) and 17th (1964) Amendments stayed valid. Earlier amendments were NOT cancelled.

sections.heading: Article 31C: what it protects and what was struck down

blocks.title: Article 31C (inserted by 25th Amendment, 1971): two parts
head: Part
What it said
What happened
rows: No law implementing Art 39(b) (distribution of material resources of the community) or Art 39(c) (no concentration of wealth) shall be void because it violates Art 14, Art 19 or Art 31.
Upheld in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973). Still valid today, as a shield against Art 14 and Art 19.
No law that DECLARES it gives effect to this policy can be questioned in court on the ground that it does not actually give effect to it.
Struck down in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), because judicial review is a basic feature.
The first part was extended to laws implementing ANY Directive Principle in Part IV.
Struck down in the Minerva Mills case (1980).
Art 31 (right to property) was omitted, so the reference to Art 31 also left Art 31C.
Art 31C now protects only against Art 14 and Art 19.

blocks.title: Conditions and limits
items: The protection is ONLY against challenges under Art 14 and Art 19. It does not protect a law against Art 21, Art 25 or any other right.

A State law gets Art 31C protection only if it is reserved for the President's consideration and receives the President's assent. The Governor's assent alone is not enough. The same rule applies to Art 31A.
Without that assent, the law just loses the special shield; it is not automatically invalid. It is tested like any other law.
A declaration in the law (for example in its preamble) does not stop the court from checking whether it really serves Art 39(b) or (c).
Art 39(b) and Art 39(c) are called 'socialistic' Directive Principles.

head: Article
Heading
Added by
Shield
rows: Saving of laws providing for acquisition of estates, etc. It covers 5 categories: taking over estates, the State taking over management of property, merger of corporations, changing rights of directors or shareholders, and ending mining leases
Against Art 14 and Art 19. A State law needs the President's assent. The 17th Amendment (1964) added market-value compensation for land a person cultivates himself, within the ceiling limit.
Validation of Acts and Regulations in the Ninth Schedule
Against all Fundamental Rights. But laws added after 24 April 1973 can be tested in court (Waman Rao case, I.R. Coelho case)
Saving of laws giving effect to certain Directive Principles
Against Art 14 and Art 19, for laws implementing Art 39(b) and Art 39(c). A State law needs the President's assent
Not enforceable by courts, but fundamental in the governance of the country

blocks.title: Amendments (chronological)
head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: Added the Ninth Schedule, Art 31A and Art 31B. Also added Art 15(4)
Added a safeguard to Art 31A: market-value compensation for land a person cultivates himself, within the ceiling limit
Parliament can amend any Fundamental Right
Extended Art 31C to all Directive Principles. Added clauses (4) and (5) to Art 368
Deleted the right to property from Part III (Art 31 and Art 19(1)(f)). Added Art 300A (property became a legal right outside Part III)

blocks.title: What the Supreme Court said
head: Who said it
What was said
rows: The Constitution rests on the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles. They are 'like two wheels of a chariot, one no less than the other'. Giving absolute primacy to one disturbs the harmony. This harmony and balance is an essential feature of the basic structure. The goals of the Directive Principles must be reached without destroying the means given by the Fundamental Rights.

blocks.title: Present position (Laxmikanth)
items: Fundamental Rights are supreme over Directive Principles.
But Art 14 and Art 19 give way to the Directive Principles in Art 39(b) and Art 39(c), because of Art 31C.
Parliament CAN amend Fundamental Rights to implement Directive Principles, as long as the amendment does not damage the basic structure.
Courts use harmonious construction: read both Parts together so that effect is given to both.
So today's position is NOT just a repeat of Champakam Dorairajan (1951); it is the balance of Minerva Mills.
Directive Principles cannot override all Fundamental Rights.
As of Nov 2026: in the Property Owners Association case (2024), the Supreme Court held that Art 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda, still works.

sections.heading: Directive Principles inside Fundamental Rights cases

head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Right to education at every level, including medicine and engineering, is part of Art 21 (read with Art 41). Charging a capitation fee (extra money for admission) violates Art 14.
Went too far, so it was partly overruled the next year (Unni Krishnan case).
Free education is a right only until a child completes 14 years. After that, it depends on the State's economic capacity and development. Art 21 read with Art 41, 45 and 46.
Led to Art 21A by the 86th Amendment (2002).

A Kerala law giving workers paid national and festival holidays was challenged under Art 19(1)(g). The Court upheld it as a reasonable restriction under Art 19(6), using Art 43 (living wage and leisure for workers) to judge reasonableness.
Directive Principles help courts decide whether a restriction is 'reasonable'. They do not give a law blanket (total) immunity.

items: Art 41: right to work and public assistance, within the State's economic capacity (a Directive Principle).
Art 21A separately guarantees free and compulsory education for ages 6 to 14 (a Fundamental Right).

Directive Principles guide courts when they check laws. Courts can uphold social-justice laws that remove economic inequality, give workers a decent standard of living, or protect weaker sections. But courts never uphold a law that is placed beyond all court checking.

The Supreme Court is the final interpreter and guardian of the Constitution (Laxmikanth). Courts use Directive Principles when interpreting laws (as in the MRF case, 1998). But the Supreme Court cannot change the Preamble on its own, because only Parliament can amend the Constitution under Art 368.
A law promoting a Fundamental Duty can still be tested against Fundamental Rights.
The Golaknath case was decided in 1967, not 1971. It never made Directive Principles enforceable.
The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) struck down only the SECOND part of Art 31C, not all of it.
The Minerva Mills case (1980) struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Art 31C. It did NOT strike down the original Art 31C, and NOT the whole 42nd Amendment.
Art 368 clauses (4) and (5) came from the 42nd Amendment (1976), not the 44th.
Art 31C shields a law against Art 14 and Art 19 only, never against Art 21.
A State law needs the President's assent to get protection under Art 31A or Art 31C.
Fundamental Rights rest on legal sanction; Directive Principles on moral and political sanction.
Fundamental Rights promote individual welfare; Directive Principles promote community welfare.

subcards.title: Fundamental Duties (Article 51A)
subcards.summary: The 11 duties every citizen owes the nation, and how they work.
at_a_glance: Art 51A — the only Article in Part IVA
42nd Amendment (1976): 10 duties; in force from 3 January 1977
86th Amendment (2002): Art 51A(k) — parent or guardian to give education opportunities to a child aged 6–14
Swaran Singh Committee (1976), which suggested 8 duties
Constitution of the former USSR (Soviet Union)
Non-justiciable (a court cannot be asked to enforce them directly); but Parliament can make laws to enforce them

sections.heading: How Fundamental Duties came into the Constitution

items: The original Constitution (1950) had Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles (duties of the State), but no list of duties of citizens.
The framers (the makers of the Constitution) did not think such a list was needed. Ten duties were added only in 1976, and one more in 2002.

The idea came from the Constitution of the former USSR (Soviet Union). It said that citizens' use of their rights cannot be separated from performing their duties. Socialist countries gave equal importance to rights and duties.

Major democracies such as the USA, Canada, France, Germany and Australia have no specific list of citizens' duties in their Constitutions. Japan's Constitution is perhaps the only democratic Constitution with such a list.
If asked 'which was the first country to put Fundamental Duties in its Constitution?', the expected answer is the USSR. India was NOT the first.

blocks.title: Swaran Singh Committee (1976)
head: Point
Fact
rows: The Congress Party (Indira Gandhi's government) in 1976, during the internal Emergency (1975–77). It was NOT set up by the later Janata government.
Sardar Swaran Singh. Members included H.R. Gokhale, A.R. Antulay, C.M. Stephen, Dinesh Goswami. M.N. Venkatachaliah was NOT a member (he later headed the 2000 Constitution Review Commission).
Add a separate chapter on Fundamental Duties, so citizens know that along with rights they also have duties
8 duties. But the 42nd Amendment actually added 10.

(1) Parliament may punish people who do not follow the duties. (2) Such a punishing law cannot be challenged in any court on the ground that it violates Fundamental Rights or any other provision. (3) Paying taxes should be a duty.

items.what: Swaran Singh Committee recommends duties; 42nd Amendment Act passed
items.detail: It added Part IVA, which has only one Article (Art 51A) listing 10 duties. The Congress party called the earlier absence of duties a 'historical mistake'.

items.what: Part IVA (original 10 duties) comes into force
items.detail: This was while the Emergency was still on — it was lifted only in March 1977.

items.what: The Janata Government (Prime Minister Morarji Desai) undid many changes of the 42nd Amendment through the 43rd and 44th Amendments — but did NOT remove the duties
items.detail: This shows that all sides finally agreed the duties are useful.

items.what: Justice J.S. Verma Committee on Fundamental Duties of Citizens reports

The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (chairman M.N. Venkatachaliah) suggests making people aware of the duties, and adding new duties: to vote, to take part actively in democracy, and to pay taxes
items.detail: These new duties have NOT been added to Art 51A.

items.what: 86th Amendment Act becomes law: it adds the 11th duty, Art 51A(k)
items.detail: The same Act also added Art 21A (Fundamental Right to education) and changed Art 45.

items.what: Art 51A(k) and Art 21A come into force (with the Right to Education Act)
items.detail: So from April 2010 this duty is backed by a statutory right (a right given by an Act of Parliament — the Right to Education Act, 2009).

blocks.title: Who said what
head: Person
Said
rows: Before the Emergency, some people did not respect the legal order. The duties would have a 'sobering effect on these restless spirits' (would calm down those who kept agitating against the law).
Duties are not meant to crush rights but to create a 'democratic balance' — people should be as aware of their duties as they are of their rights.

sections.heading: The 11 duties of Article 51A (and what is NOT a duty)

blocks.text: Art 51A: 'It shall be the duty of every citizen of India' —

head: Clause
Duty (Constitution's words)
Example situation
rows: Abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem
National Flag used as a cover for a speaker's desk at a private party — violates 51A(a)
Cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom
Uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
Defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so
Only 'when called upon' — there is no fixed compulsory service. For example, '5 years of national service' is NOT a duty.

Promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood among all people of India, transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities; and renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women
Calming a fight that started over anti-religious remarks. Note: the duty about the dignity of women is in clause (e), not clause (k).
Value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture
Documenting and preserving different cultural traditions
Protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and have compassion for living creatures
Teaching how to make compost at home for a park. The clause says both 'protect' and 'improve'; compassion for living creatures is in the same clause.
Develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform
All four: scientific temper, humanism, inquiry, reform
Safeguard public property and abjure (give up) violence
Students writing their names on the walls of Humayun's Tomb (violation); protecting public buses during a protest (following the duty). It covers PUBLIC property only — not private houses.
Strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity, so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement
For every citizen, not only public office holders
Who is a parent or guardian, to provide opportunities for education to his child or ward (a child in the guardian's care) between the age of 6 and 14 years (added by the 86th Amendment, 2002)
Construction worker taking his 8-year-old son to the site instead of school

blocks.title: NOT Fundamental Duties (common wrong options)
head: Option
Where it actually is
rows: Vote in elections / exercise adult franchise
Not a duty. The right to vote comes from Art 326 (adult suffrage), which is outside Part III, so it is not a Fundamental Right. The details are in the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
Not a duty. The Swaran Singh Committee suggested it, but it was not accepted. Still, a tax validly imposed by law must be paid — that is a legal duty under the tax law.
Not a duty. 'Population control and family planning' is a subject in the Concurrent List (subjects on which both Parliament and State legislatures can make laws).
Protect weaker sections from social injustice; promote the educational and economic interests of weaker sections, especially Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs)
This is a Directive Principle (a duty of the State) — Art 46
Public assistance in old age, sickness, disablement
This is a Directive Principle (a duty of the State) — Art 41
Respect elders; protect elderly, differently abled and children
Not in Art 51A (a moral duty only)
Not a duty — Art 51A(i) speaks only of PUBLIC property
Not a duty — Art 51A(d) says national service only 'when called upon'

blocks.title: Same value elsewhere in the Constitution
head: Duty
Matching provision
rows: Art 48A — a Directive Principle asking the State to protect the environment
Art 21A — Fundamental Right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14. Art 51A(k) adds a duty on the parent; it does NOT replace the State's duty under Art 21A.

Art 24: no child below 14 may work in a factory, mine or other hazardous work — this applies to private factories too. Art 45: the State should provide early childhood care and education for children until age 6.

sections.heading: Nature and features of the duties

head: Feature
Meaning
rows: A moral duty rests on a person's conscience — for example, cherishing the ideals of the freedom struggle. A civic duty is a duty owed as a citizen — for example, respecting the Constitution, the National Flag and the National Anthem.
They write down (codify) values that were already part of Indian tradition, religions and way of life. But just because a value is traditional, breaking it does not become a crime.

Art 51A speaks to 'every citizen of India'. No duty, not even Art 51A(i), applies to foreigners. By contrast, some Fundamental Rights — Articles 14, 20, 21, 21A and 22 to 28 — are available to foreigners too.

Like Directive Principles, courts cannot directly enforce them. No writ (court order) can be issued to force a person to perform a duty, and the Constitution itself gives no penalty for breaking them. That is why they were not put in Part III, whose rights are justiciable (enforceable in court).

Parliament can make laws (statutes) to enforce them and punish those who break them. Courts also take the duties into account while deciding cases. But such a law must still respect Fundamental Rights.
Part IVA has only ONE Article — Art 51A — not 11 Articles. Part IV (Directive Principles) is addressed to the State, while Art 51A is addressed to citizens.

blocks.title: Legal duty vs moral duty
head: Aspect
Legal duty
Moral duty
rows: Pay a tax imposed by law

blocks.title: Rights and duties
items: Rights and duties are correlative (they go together) and cannot be separated.
Rights are claims of citizens against the State.

Rights used without concern for others make people irresponsible. Duties imposed without freedom make people mere subordinates. So a balance is needed — duties cannot simply wipe out rights whenever the State wishes.
Mahatma Gandhi: 'The true source of rights is duty. If we all discharge our duties, rights will not be far to seek.'

International link: Fundamental Duties are in line with Art 29(1) of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR, 1948), which says everyone has duties to the community. Art 29(2) adds that rights may be limited only by limits 'determined by law' — so a restriction in the name of duty still needs a legal basis.
Besides Fundamental Rights, the Preamble, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties also reflect UDHR principles.

blocks.title: Criticism
head: Criticism
Explanation
rows: The list leaves out duties like voting, paying taxes and family planning. The Swaran Singh Committee had in fact recommended paying taxes.
Phrases like 'noble ideals', 'composite culture', 'scientific temper', 'spirit of inquiry' can be read in many ways.
Critics call them a code of moral precepts (moral advice only), because they are non-justiciable and carry no direct legal punishment. The Swaran Singh Committee had suggested penalties.
People would perform these duties anyway, even without listing them.
They were added as an appendage (a tail-end attachment) to Part IV, which lowers their value. Critics say they should have come right after Part III, on par with Fundamental Rights.

blocks.title: Critics' words
head: Critic
Point
rows: Duties are vague — 'one is left guessing the noble ideals'. The meaning of 'composite culture' and 'scientific temper' is unclear.
Over 99.9% of citizens are law-abiding; telling them their duties is unnecessary (superfluous).
The people created the Republic, but now the State behaves like a 'harsh school master' over the people. His concern: in a democracy the people are the real masters (popular sovereignty).

blocks.title: Significance
items: They remind citizens that while enjoying rights, they also owe duties to the country, society and fellow citizens.
They warn against anti-national and anti-social acts, like burning the National Flag or destroying public property.
They inspire discipline and commitment, so citizens become active participants in national goals, not mere spectators.

They help courts decide whether a law is constitutional. In the Mohan Kumar Singhania case (1991), the Supreme Court held that Art 51A can be used to interpret unclear (ambiguous) laws. In the Ramlila Maidan case (2012), it said a common thread runs through Parts III, IV and IVA.
They are enforceable by law: Parliament can make laws to punish failure to perform them.
Even though courts cannot enforce them directly, they can still be used for civic education and as a guide for government policy.

sections.heading: Verma Committee (1999) and laws that already enforce the duties

blocks.text: The Verma Committee on Fundamental Duties of Citizens (1999, headed by Justice J.S. Verma) worked on how to teach the duties and put them into practice. It found that laws ALREADY existed to implement some duties:

head: Law (year)
What it does
Duty it supports
rows: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (1971)
Punishes disrespect to the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem
Criminal laws, including the Indian Penal Code (IPC)
Punish promoting enmity (hatred) between groups on grounds of language, race, place of birth or religion; the Indian Penal Code also punishes statements harmful to national integration
Protection of Civil Rights Act (1955) — called the Untouchability (Offences) Act until 1976
Punishes offences related to caste and religion, such as practising untouchability
Allows the government to declare a communal organisation an unlawful association (a banned body)
Disqualifies Members of Parliament and State legislatures for corrupt practices — such as seeking votes on the ground of religion, or promoting enmity between sections of people
Bans trade in rare and endangered species of wildlife
Checks careless cutting of forests and the use of forest land for non-forest purposes. In 2023 it was renamed the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980.

head: Law
Year
rows: Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act

head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986)
Students (Jehovah's Witnesses) who stood up respectfully but did not sing the National Anthem could not be expelled; the Supreme Court set aside their expulsion
Standing respectfully is enough; no one can be forced to sing the Anthem
Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of UP (1986)
Preserving the environment and the ecological balance is a task of governments and also of every citizen (his duty under Art 51A(g))
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1991)

Relying on Art 51A(g), the Supreme Court directed: compulsory environment education in schools, step by step up to matriculation or intermediate level; the University Grants Commission (UGC) to make universities prescribe environment courses; and daily environment messages in cinema halls, on All India Radio and on Doordarshan
A duty was used as the basis for court directions
Mohan Kumar Singhania v. Union of India (1991)
Art 51A can be used to interpret unclear (ambiguous) laws while deciding whether they are constitutional
Common trap: this was NOT the Kesavananda Bharati case
Duties cannot be enforced by a writ, but they are as important as Fundamental Rights and are a valuable guide for interpreting constitutional and legal questions
Courts can rely on duties while deciding cases
Ranganath Mishra v. Union of India (2003)
Directed the Central Government to act on the Verma Committee's suggestions for teaching the duties and spreading awareness about them
Put the Verma Committee's ideas into action
A common thread runs through Parts III, IV and IVA, so they should be interpreted together
Rights, Directive Principles and duties are read together

items: When a court tests a law under Art 14 or Art 19, it may treat the law as 'reasonable' if the law gives effect to a Fundamental Duty.
But such a law can still be checked to see whether it violates Fundamental Rights.

blocks.title: Amendments
head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: Added Part IVA (Fundamental Duties), Art 39A (free legal aid) and Part XIVA (tribunals — the Swaran Singh Committee had also recommended administrative tribunals). It extended the term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies from 5 to 6 years. It did NOT replace 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' in Art 352 — that was done by the 44th Amendment (1978).
Added the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law — stops legislators from switching parties)
Added Art 21A (right to education), changed Art 45, and added Art 51A(k) (the 11th duty)

blocks.title: Parts
head: Part
Content
rows: Directive Principles — for example, Art 50 (keep the judiciary separate from the executive) and Art 51 (promote international peace)

blocks.text: Which category? Equal pay for equal work is a Directive Principle (Art 39(d)). Life and personal liberty is a Fundamental Right (Art 21). Safeguarding public property is a Fundamental Duty (Art 51A(i)). The right to vote by adult suffrage is a constitutional right outside Part III (Art 326). Also: Art 42 is about just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief; Art 43 is about a living wage for workers.

items: The Swaran Singh Committee suggested 8 duties; the 42nd Amendment added 10; today there are 11.
The 11th duty is Art 51A(k), added by the 86th Amendment (2002) and in force from 1 April 2010. The duty is on the parent or guardian.
Part IVA has only one Article (Art 51A). It came into force on 3 January 1977, during the Emergency.
These are NOT Fundamental Duties: voting, paying taxes, family planning, protecting weaker sections, respecting elders, protecting private property.
Duties apply only to citizens — even Art 51A(i) does not cover foreigners.
Duties are non-justiciable, but Parliament can enforce them by law. The Swaran Singh Committee's proposal for penalties was NOT accepted.
Using Art 51A to interpret unclear laws = Mohan Kumar Singhania case (1991), NOT Kesavananda Bharati.
Verma Committee (1999) found that existing laws already enforce some duties. The Constitution Review Commission (2000) suggested making people aware of duties and adding duties to vote and pay taxes.
